key_insight: A personalised “normative twin” model of heart shape reveals hidden, reproducible deviation patterns that conventional cardiac biomarkers miss and that map to different future risk profiles.
clinical_relevance: This approach could improve risk stratification in people with preserved ejection fraction, especially for predicting incident atrial fibrillation and, in a separate model, stroke.
method: Compared each patient’s cardiac shape to an age-, sex-, and body-habitus-matched healthy digital twin.
Learned deviation patterns from two independent shape representations: HeartSSM (128D) and MeshHeart cVAE (64D).
Tested whether deviation scores added predictive value beyond standard biomarkers and against placebo noise controls.
evidence_signal: In UK Biobank cohorts, the method improved prediction beyond ejection fraction, volumes, mass, and strain; the strongest result was for incident atrial fibrillation in preserved-EF individuals (ΔC = +0.068, cross-validated ΔC = +0.063, P = 3.3 × 10^-8), with a smaller independent signal for stroke in the other representation.
watch_item: Generalizability and clinical deployment still need careful validation across sites, imaging pipelines, and populations before routine use.
paper_title: Personalised normative cardiac phenotyping reveals clinically relevant heterogeneity in cardiac shape and outcome risk
